strengths: The paper presents a simple, intuitive, and computationally lightweight consensus signal: selecting preference pairs according to semantic centrality among self-generated responses.
The empirical study covers six base models from two model families, four translation directions, two summarization datasets, and both DPO- and GRPO-based training.
SVSI improves over the base model consistently in the reported main table and is generally more stable than self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines, which often suffer severe degradation.

The flipped-preference experiment is a useful validation showing that the ordering induced by semantic voting contains meaningful information rather than merely triggering improvement through arbitrary training.

Ablations investigate clustering, embedding models, clustering algorithms, sampling parameters, and clustering hyperparameters; limited out-of-distribution translation results also provide some evidence of transfer.
The approach substantially reduces preference-label construction time relative to methods requiring additional LLM inference.
weaknesses: The novelty is only moderate: average embedding similarity effectively selects a semantic medoid and is closely related to minimum-Bayes-risk, consensus-decoding, and semantic self-consistency methods, yet these literatures and corresponding baselines are largely absent. This weakens both positioning and evidence that the contribution is more than a straightforward adaptation.

The evaluation reports essentially point estimates without repeated-run variance or statistical significance for the main DPO results. This is important because pseudo-label construction, generation, and fine-tuning are stochastic, and several gains are small.

Baseline coverage is insufficient. There is no random-pair DPO control, winner-only SFT/rejection-sampling baseline, direct minimum-Bayes-risk or semantic-consistency baseline, or stronger externally evaluated preference construction. The selected self-judging baseline is particularly disadvantaged for the 1B–3B models, which may have weak judging ability.

The efficiency comparison measures only preference-pair construction, omitting the 64 response generations and subsequent training that may dominate total cost. Hardware, batching, and timing protocol are not reported, so the claimed orders-of-magnitude end-to-end efficiency advantage is not established.

Experimental and reproducibility details remain incomplete: dataset split sizes and resulting numbers of valid preference pairs are missing; parsing rejection rates are unreported; it is unclear whether training is full-parameter or parameter-efficient; and the precise entropy computation, self-judge prompt, hardware, and handling of clustering failures, noise points, and ties are unspecified.

The primary evaluation is transductive test-time training and testing on the same unlabeled input set. Although labels are not used, this should be distinguished more clearly from general capability improvement. The out-of-distribution study covers only two small models and translation, with some regressions, so the broader self-improvement claim is stronger than the evidence.

Reliance on embedding consensus can reward generic, mutually similar, or commonly repeated errors rather than faithfulness to the source. This failure mode is not directly measured through human evaluation, factuality tests, source-conditioned similarity, or analysis of pseudo-preference accuracy.

Metric reporting is under-specified: n-MQM and BLEURT values appear scaled but the scaling is not stated, and automatic metrics alone are insufficient to validate translation adequacy and summarization factuality. No human evaluation is provided.

There are minor technical imprecisions: cosine similarity is declared to map to [0,1] although it generally lies in [-1,1], Equation 2 divides an N-1-term sum by N, and the description conflates cosine similarity with a clustering distance.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly organized, and the semantic-voting pipeline is simple to understand and implement. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3e6f4a100f764d09ae0e045397bdbda5/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation covers six Llama/Qwen models, four translation directions, two summarization datasets, two metric families, and several embedding, clustering, and hyperparameter ablations.

SVSI is generally more stable than the self-judging and entropy-minimization implementations. The flipped-preference experiment and limited out-of-distribution translation evaluation are useful diagnostic additions.
weaknesses: The core method has limited novelty. Selecting the candidate with greatest average similarity is essentially centroid/medoid-style consensus or minimum-Bayes-risk selection, yet the paper does not adequately position itself against semantic self-consistency, consensus decoding, or MBR literature. Clustering followed by DPO is a relatively incremental combination.

The central causal claim is insufficiently validated. No human evaluation, reference-based preference-accuracy analysis, or correlation study establishes that semantic-voting scores actually represent response quality. A flipped-SV model performing worse only shows that reversing a mode-seeking signal is harmful; it does not establish that the original preferences are correct.

The baseline suite is too narrow for the claimed contribution. Important controls include random-pair DPO, ordinary self-training/SFT, direct consensus or MBR decoding, embedding-based selection without DPO, and stronger external or reference-based preference construction. The paper also provides insufficient evidence that the weak-model self-judging baseline was implemented and tuned competitively.

The main evaluation adapts models on the same test inputs on which performance is reported. This transductive test-time setting is materially weaker evidence than conventional held-out evaluation. The appendix evaluates out-of-distribution transfer only for translation and two 1B models, with non-universal gains, leaving the broader generalization claims unsupported.

Results lack repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main DPO experiments. Several reported gains are very small, and SVSI is not uniformly superior: for example, Llama-3B often benefits more from entropy minimization, while Llama-3B PubMed ROUGE-L slightly declines relative to the base model. Thus claims of consistent improvement and overall superiority are overstated.

The efficiency comparison measures only preference-pair construction and omits the shared but likely dominant costs of sampling 64 responses per input and DPO training. Hardware, batching, exact timing values, and uncertainty are not reported, so the broader computational-efficiency claim is not well supported.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete in the manuscript, including training-set sizes and splits for translation, random seeds, the full self-judging prompt and tie handling, precise entropy scoring and preference direction, invalid-output rates, and clustering failure handling. The surprising complete parsing failures for some Qwen summarization settings also suggest substantial sensitivity to prompting and formatting.

The method is described as unsupervised and self-evaluation-free, but it relies on a separately supervised sentence-embedding model. Moreover, response-only similarity ignores the source document or source sentence, so a cluster of mutually similar hallucinations or mistranslations can receive high scores. This limitation is central to the proposed signal but is not directly investigated.

There are smaller technical imprecisions: cosine similarity is declared to map to [0,1] although it can be negative, and the stated averaging denominator includes the candidate itself even though the corresponding term is excluded. These do not change the ranking but weaken the formal presentation. Overall, the promising empirical pattern does not compensate for the limited novelty, incomplete controls, and weak evidence that semantic consensus reliably measures correctness.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, intuitive, and practically useful idea: approximate majority voting for open-ended responses using embedding-based semantic centrality, followed by preference optimization.
The empirical study is broad, covering six Llama/Qwen models, four translation directions, two summarization datasets, lexical and semantic metrics, and an out-of-distribution translation evaluation.

SVSI is substantially more stable than the self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines in the reported main results; notably, it avoids the severe collapses those baselines exhibit in several configurations.

The flipped-preference experiment, component ablations, hyperparameter studies, alternative embedding models, alternative clustering algorithms, and GRPO extension provide useful evidence that the semantic-voting signal is meaningful and reasonably robust.
The approach is lightweight and potentially valuable in settings where additional LLM judging is prohibitively expensive.
weaknesses: The novelty is modest and insufficiently positioned. Selecting a semantic medoid or centroid-like response from embedding similarities is a natural extension of consistency-based selection, yet the paper does not compare carefully against prior semantic-consistency, embedding-clustering, or open-ended self-consistency methods. The claim that majority voting is strictly limited to exact-match tasks is too strong.

The experimental protocol lacks essential information: the number and selection of adaptation examples are not reported, it is unclear whether evaluation inputs are exactly the same inputs used to construct DPO pairs, and the main table provides no repeated-seed results, variance, or significance tests. This is especially concerning because stochastic generation, clustering, and DPO can all introduce substantial variability.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics. There is no human assessment or direct validation that voting scores correlate with correctness, adequacy, factuality, or preference quality. Semantic centrality can favor generic summaries or consensus mistranslations, which BLEURT/MetricX and the embedding-based selector may not adequately expose.

The baseline set is incomplete. Random preference pairs, random selection within the largest cluster, response-level SFT, oracle metric-selected pairs, and stronger semantic-clustering/consistency baselines would help isolate whether gains arise from semantic voting specifically, clustering, additional training, or generic self-generated preference optimization.

The headline efficiency comparison is under-specified: hardware, batching, implementation, and whether generation-time logits are retained are not documented. Entropy can often be accumulated during generation, so recomputing it afterward may exaggerate SVSI's advantage. End-to-end costs, including generation and DPO training, are also omitted.

Several technical and reproducibility details remain ambiguous, including handling of HDBSCAN noise and tied/largest clusters, examples with too few valid boxed generations, preferred and dispreferred samples becoming identical, exact training-set sizes, and whether DPO operates on parsed answers or full reasoning traces. In addition, cosine similarity is stated to map to [0,1], although its standard range is [-1,1].

Overall, the results are promising and the paper is well developed, but the limited novelty positioning and gaps in experimental controls prevent the evidence from clearly crossing the top-tier acceptance threshold. strengths: The proposed semantic-voting signal is simple, intuitive, inexpensive, and easy to integrate with DPO or GRPO.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering six Llama/Qwen models, translation and summarization, multiple embedding and clustering choices, and an out-of-distribution evaluation.
The paper includes useful ablations of clustering and semantic voting, reversed-preference experiments, hyperparameter studies, and an analysis acknowledging reduced output diversity.
SVSI generally improves upon the base models and appears more stable than the implemented self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited: selecting a semantic medoid through average embedding similarity is a straightforward extension of self-consistency and is closely related to minimum-Bayes-risk decoding and semantic-consensus methods, yet these connections and corresponding baselines are not adequately discussed.

The main evaluation is transductive: models are trained using self-generated responses for the evaluation inputs and then evaluated on those same inputs. The limited out-of-distribution study covers only translation and two small models, so it does not fully support claims of general self-improvement.

The baseline set is too narrow. There is no random-pair DPO control, MBR or semantic-consensus decoding baseline, pseudo-label SFT baseline, or reference/oracle preference upper bound. Flipping preferences does not establish that semantic voting is better than generic DPO on self-generated samples.

Results rely almost entirely on automatic metrics, despite emphasizing unverifiable open-ended tasks. Human evaluation is absent, and the instruction-following appendix uses only one LLM judge without uncertainty analysis.

Main results appear to be single runs without confidence intervals or significance tests. This is particularly problematic because preference construction, generation, and training are stochastic, and the GRPO experiments themselves reveal substantial instability.

The efficiency claim measures only preference-pair construction, omitting the shared cost of generating 64 responses per input and subsequent training. Hardware, batching, input-length controls, and uncertainty are also missing, so the claimed orders-of-magnitude end-to-end advantage is not established.

Several reporting choices are unclear or potentially misleading: n-MQM and BLEURT appear rescaled without stating the scale; percentage improvements become ill-defined or inflated for zero or near-zero base scores; dataset and training-pair sizes are incompletely reported; and some base models produce no valid outputs.

The method explicitly reduces semantic diversity, but the proposed remedy of increasing sampling temperature is not experimentally validated and may conflict with the paper's own finding that higher temperatures degrade semantic-voting performance.

strengths: The core method is simple, intuitive, and computationally attractive: semantic consensus provides a lightweight alternative to repeatedly invoking an LLM as its own evaluator.

The empirical study covers six base models, translation and summarization tasks, two optimization frameworks, multiple embedding and clustering choices, flipped-preference controls, and limited out-of-distribution evaluation.
The paper openly reports important limitations, including unstable GRPO training, sensitivity for weaker models, and reduced linguistic diversity.
The ablations generally support the claim that semantic voting contributes information beyond clustering alone.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is transductive: the models are tuned using the same test inputs on which improvements are measured. This substantially weakens claims of capability improvement. The out-of-distribution study is restricted to translation and only two small models, with some regressions, so it does not adequately repair this issue.

Evaluation is heavily confounded by output formatting and parsing. Several capable base models receive zero scores or produce no valid summaries, while self-judging sometimes causes near-total collapse. Valid-output rates are not reported, making it unclear how much of the measured gain reflects semantic quality rather than format compliance or recovery from a problematic prompt/parser.

The method is technically straightforward—essentially selecting the semantic medoid and an outlying response within the largest embedding cluster—and its novelty is overstated. Positioning against closely related semantic-consistency, minimum-Bayes-risk, consensus-decoding, and semantic-entropy approaches is insufficient.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. The paper lacks random-pair DPO, random or likelihood-based selection, supervised-oracle upper bounds, consensus/MBR baselines, and a direct comparison to cluster-based methods under the same DPO setup. Consequently, the source of improvement is not cleanly isolated.

The principal tables provide results from apparently single runs without uncertainty estimates or significance tests, despite stochastic generation and training. Claims of consistency and stability are therefore not well supported.

Automatic metrics are the sole substantive quality evidence. The reported Kendall correlations with MetricX are low, approximately 0.10–0.24, and MetricX is then also used for translation evaluation. There is no human assessment showing that consensus actually selects more faithful, less generic, or less hallucinated outputs.

The efficiency comparison measures only preference-pair construction, lacks enough timing and hardware detail, and deemphasizes the shared cost of sampling 64 responses per input. Thus, the headline orders-of-magnitude efficiency claim does not establish end-to-end training efficiency.

Several technical details are imprecise: cosine similarity is stated to lie in [0,1] although it can be negative; the average in the voting equation divides by the cluster size despite excluding the candidate itself; and the displayed n-MQM scale does not match the stated formula unless an unreported factor of 100 is applied.

Reproducibility information remains incomplete, including exact training/evaluation splits and sizes for the translation datasets, random seeds, variance across runs, training implementation details, baseline prompts, invalid-output handling, and full timing methodology.

SVSI measurably reduces semantic diversity, yet the paper dismisses possible model-collapse concerns without iterative experiments. Suggesting that increased sampling temperature solves the issue is also in tension with the paper's own finding that higher temperatures degrade SVSI.

strengths: Semantic voting is a simple, intuitive, and practically useful alternative to LLM-based self-evaluation: selecting responses by embedding-space consensus substantially reduces preference-construction cost.

The empirical scope is strong, covering six Llama/Qwen models, translation and summarization, lexical and semantic metrics, several embedding and clustering choices, back-translation, out-of-distribution evaluation, and an instruction-following benchmark.
SVSI improves over every reported base-model configuration and is generally more stable than self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines, several of which suffer severe degradation.

The flipped-preference experiment, component ablations, ranking-correlation analysis, hyperparameter studies, and GRPO extension provide useful evidence that the semantic signal—not merely additional self-training—contributes to the gains.
The paper is clearly motivated and written, and the method is straightforward to implement using standard embedding, clustering, and DPO components.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the core score is essentially embedding-space centrality or medoid selection followed by standard DPO. Comparisons with closely related consensus alternatives—such as cluster-size rewards under the same DPO pipeline, centroid/medoid selection, random-pair DPO, and SFT on consensus responses—are incomplete.

The main results apparently come from single runs and report neither uncertainty nor significance. This is important because many improvements are small, DPO can be seed-sensitive, and the GRPO experiments explicitly reveal substantial run-to-run variability.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic metrics and includes no human assessment. Moreover, the MetricX-based validation is only a proxy for true quality, and its reported Kendall values are modest (roughly 0.10–0.24) and confusingly displayed as percentages rather than coefficients.

The experimental protocol needs greater clarity: the main setting adapts on the evaluation inputs themselves, training-set sizes for the translation experiments are not stated, and invalid-format rates are omitted. Some zero/NA summarization results suggest that formatting failures may materially affect comparisons.

The efficiency analysis measures only preference-pair construction, lacks hardware and uncertainty details, and excludes the shared cost of generating 64 responses per input. It therefore supports lower scoring overhead, but not as clearly the broader claim of highly efficient self-improvement.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including random seeds, hardware, whether tuning is full-parameter or parameter-efficient, exact per-dataset training sizes, and selection rules for ties or failed clustering. The method also consistently reduces semantic diversity, a limitation that deserves a more substantive treatment than the proposed temperature-based mitigation.
